name: The Mansion House's Stable

documented_range.note: COPIED FROM THE HOUSE IT SERVES (data/structures/mansion_house.json, phase log_frame_1833, 1833-01-01 to 1850-12-31). No source dates this building, because no source mentions it. The stable is taken to stand while the house kept travellers, because keeping a traveller's horse overnight was a priced service of a Chicago tavern from the county's first licences on (the 1831 order below). If the house kept its horses at a livery or a neighbour's barn instead, this range is wrong in the only way that matters: the building was not there. T-1776.

change_note: A stable behind the Mansion House, sized from the beds the lodging model gives the house and placed on its own ground. T-1776.

placement.position_note: NOTHING PLACES THIS BUILDING AND THIS COORDINATE IS A CHOICE, bounded by the lot. The placement policy's ancillary clause (`ancillary_behind_its_own_roof`: stables 'go off the block alley behind the roof they serve') and the house's own footprint decide where it may go; inside that, it is the alley end of blk_south_water_dearborn lot #01, the Mansion House's own lot: 1.5 m inside the alley line (plat_occupancy's LOT_MARGIN_M) at the alley's west end, and 3.3 m inside the lot's Dearborn line, square behind the house. Checked against every committed footprint with a 1 m clearance and against the modelled water; nothing was hit. L317. MOVED 2026-10-04 WITH THE HOUSE IT SERVES (T-1679): the Mansion House now stands on lot #03, plat lot 6, one lot east, and the clause that put this stable on the house's own lot moves it with the house. It keeps the same seat on its new lot — the same distance inside the alley line and inside the lot's west line — translated by the committed plat's lot-to-lot vector along the alley, (+25.92, -0.48) m local, lot 5's north-west corner 710.72,-57.14 to lot 6's 736.64,-57.62. Nothing else about it changes.
placement.symbolic_location: Rear of the Mansion House's lot, plat lot 6 of block 16 on the north side of Lake Street east of Dearborn, against the block's east-west alley.

footprint.note: INVENTED, AND SIZED FROM THE HOUSE'S BEDS. The lodging model (data/reconstruction/1835_lodging_model.json, T-1164) puts 5 in the Mansion House on an ordinary night (35 crowded), itself graded reconstructed. ONE STALL PER TWO ORDINARY GUESTS: 5 beds / 2 = 3, raised to the floor of 4 = 4 stalls. Half, because the summer of 1835's crowd came mostly by lake and many of a town house's guests arrived without a horse; the Western Hotel's 'teams as numerous as were the guests' (chicagology_prefire278) is that house's own sentence about the teamsters' road west and is not carried to a Lake Street house; one range of 4 single standing stalls 5 ft wide and 9 ft deep, a passage behind them and a mangers' run, 20 ft deep in all, plus a 6 ft bay for harness and feed at one end: 4 x 5 + 6 = 26 ft long by 20 ft deep = 7.92 x 6.1 m. The ordinary night, not the crowded one, as the beds are sized. Every factor is ours and stated so it can be replaced: an advertisement or a sale notice naming this house's stabling, a fire-loss list, or a lot-level view of the block. L317.

construction.note: NOT STATED BY ANY SOURCE. Plank, the same reading as the Western Hotel's stable of 1834 and for the same reason: by the time this house kept travellers the town's sawmills of 1832-33 were cutting boards, and a stable is the building a keeper put up quickest and cheapest. The log reading of the Wolf Point stable is the earlier date's answer and is not carried here.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.0 m is about 10 ft: a horse led in under a header with a loft for hay above the stalls, and the archetype's own size-aware default for a footprint of this size. What is inferred is the range, not the number.

door.note: THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT, as at the Wolf Point stable: a horse kept overnight is a horse led in and out, and the archetype's 'stable' door (1.35 m clear) is the opening that allows it.

door_side.note: NOT ATTESTED. The front, at bearing 0, chosen so the door faces the block alley the placement policy puts a stable's traffic on. L317.

paint.note: No source describes a finish. An unpainted plank stable behind a painted house is the ordinary reading; nothing states it either way.

function.note: A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE. The Cook County Court of County Commissioners, sitting at Chicago on 13 April 1831, 'Ordered that the following rates be allowed to tavern keepers', among them 'For each horse fed 25' and 'Keeping horse one night 50' (Andreas, scan p. 249). That order set what a licensed Chicago house might charge to keep a traveller's horse; it is read here as standing for every public house the lodging model sizes, which is an inference, because no licence for this house in particular has been read. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: a dedicated building. A horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot or at a livery up the street; this record draws the building because a house of this size on a Lake Street lot with an alley behind it is the ordinary case, and says so.

occupants.value: the house's keeper — Edward Haddock or Abram A. Markle, keeper
occupants.note: Taken to have passed with the house (data/structures/mansion_house.json's occupants). No hostler is named and no source attaches any person to this building.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.

research_note: T-1776, the second piece of T-1209: every licensed house the lodging model sizes read for its horse-keeping against its beds. This is the Mansion House's reading — 5 ordinary beds, 4 stalls. WHAT WOULD REPLACE IT: any advertisement of the house naming its stabling (the Chicago American and the Democrat of 1834-35 carry the hotels' cards), the 1839 fire-loss lists, or a lot-level reading of Wright 1834 / Hathaway 1834 for this block. docs/RESEARCH/1835_tavern_horse_keeping.md carries the ledger for all nine houses.
